title: Did 24-Hour Cable News Kill America?
summary: Josh and Chuck examine whether 24-hour cable news has damaged American politics and shared reality. They trace the Fairness Doctrine and its repeal in 1987, the rise of talk radio and Rush Limbaugh, the launch of CNN by Ted Turner in 1980 and its coverage of Challenger, the Gulf War, and later ownership changes, the founding of Fox News by Roger Ailes in 1996 and its rise after the Lewinsky scandal and 9/11, the launch of MSNBC (originally Microsoft NBC) and its pivot to opinion programming, and research on negativity, polarization, and "angertainment." They also cover the Dominion settlement, declining cable viewership and aging audiences, the cable bundle business model, and the shift to online news. The episode closes with a listener mail story about the Hindenburg episode and a sign-off. A pre-episode Canadian tour ad appears at the start.

segments.title: Canadian tour promo
segments.summary: Chuck promotes the upcoming Canadian summer tour shows in Montreal, Ottawa, and Toronto.

segments.title: Introduction
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the topic of whether 24-hour cable news has harmed the country and note the lack of positive studies on it.

segments.title: Shared reality before cable news
segments.summary: Josh describes the era of the big three network evening news. Chuck explains the value of a shared set of facts and shared national identity.

segments.title: Fairness Doctrine and its repeal
segments.summary: The FCC's origins and the Fairness Doctrine's requirements for balanced coverage and equal time. Reagan-era repeal in 1987 led to talk radio growth, especially conservative AM talk.

segments.title: Rush Limbaugh and talk radio
segments.summary: Limbaugh's national show starting in 1988 and his influence on the Republican Party, including the honorary congressional membership claim. Hosts say Fox later modeled political commentary on this.

segments.title: Ted Turner and the founding of CNN
segments.summary: CNN launched in 1980 as the first 24-hour cable news channel. Hosts pay tribute to Ted Turner, who recently died, and discuss his other ventures and philanthropy.

segments.title: CNN's live coverage and analysts
segments.summary: CNN's breaking news coverage of the Challenger, Berlin Wall, and Gulf War; criticism of its reporting from Baghdad; and the introduction of analysts and pundits that laid groundwork for opinion journalism.

segments.title: CNN ownership change and partisan turn
segments.summary: After Turner left, Time Warner's changes at CNN are described as chasing ad revenue. Hosts tie the 1990s Clinton and Gingrich rivalry to a good-versus-evil framing in politics and the end of bipartisanship.

segments.title: Real World and the 1990s media turn
segments.summary: Chuck offers a theory linking reality television, starting with The Real World in 1992, to a culture of meanness. Josh then introduces Fox News' founding in 1996 under Roger Ailes and Rupert Murdoch.

segments.title: Ailes, the Fair and Balanced slogan, and Southern strategy
segments.summary: Ailes' background as a Republican consultant and the Southern strategy. Fox's fair and balanced motto is described as a deliberate provocation, dropped in 2017 after Ailes' firing.

segments.title: Fox News rise after Lewinsky, 2000 election, and 9/11
segments.summary: Coverage of the Lewinsky scandal boosted Fox's ratings. Its coverage of the 2000 election, 9/11, and Iraq is described as openly Republican-leaning, unlike other networks.

segments.title: MSNBC launch and pivot
segments.summary: MSNBC launched in 1996 as a Microsoft and NBC partnership aimed at tech audiences, then pivoted to opinion programming to compete with Fox. Figures such as Laura Ingraham, Tucker Carlson, and Rachel Maddow passed through the network.

segments.title: Keith Olbermann and prime-time ratings
segments.summary: Keith Olbermann's 2005 Hurricane Katrina commentary on Countdown and the ratings jump that followed. Chuck describes MSNBC's prime-time attacks on opponents and ratings gains.

segments.title: Partisan slant and angertainment research
segments.summary: A 2025 UC Boulder study on what networks cover, and a Nature study on polarizing primetime shows. Hosts discuss angertainment and the neurochemistry of outrage.

segments.title: Viewing habits and all-day background TV
segments.summary: Hosts compare anecdotal habits of viewers who keep cable news on all day, with CNN mentioned as the channel most often left on.

segments.title: Misinformation and the Dominion settlement
segments.summary: Fox News' settlement of close to $800 million with Dominion Voting Systems ahead of a trial over false claims about voting systems, with Carlson and Hannity mentioned.

segments.title: Other false or overreaching reporting and filtering
segments.summary: Chuck lists conspiracy claims reported as fact on Fox, and the Rachel Maddow Russiagate coverage, which was the subject of a lawsuit she won. Both hosts discuss news filtering by all three networks.

segments.title: Media-consumption experiment and news filtering
segments.summary: A 2023 study that paid Fox viewers to watch CNN for a month, finding slight shifts in views that faded after returning to Fox. Hosts discuss the danger of what goes uncovered.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Mid-episode ad break.

segments.title: Opinion media versus journalism
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh contrast cheap opinion media with costly real journalism and describe a study of primetime tone on Fox and MSNBC, which found mostly negative language.

segments.title: Framing viewers as victims and rising partisanship
segments.summary: Chuck describes framing viewers as the protagonists. Josh cites Pew Research on rising unfavorable views of the opposing party from 1994 to 2017, and a 2022 survey on perceived immorality.

segments.title: Online echo chambers versus TV news
segments.summary: A University of Pennsylvania study found cable TV news more divisive than online news. Hosts discuss how Fox might have looked if CNN and MSNBC had stayed with traditional journalism.

segments.title: Cable news audiences and aging viewers
segments.summary: Hosts discuss how cable news still outdraws online news and that median viewer ages are in the late sixties and seventies.

segments.title: Ratings shifts and the cable bundle business model
segments.summary: Fox's primetime viewership declined about 21 percent, MSNBC (now MS NOW) rose 15 percent, and CNN rose 46 percent in the cited period. Newsmax, NewsNation, and One America News are cited as drawing audiences from Fox. Chuck explains how cable carriage fees fund channels and why cord cutting threatens them.

segments.title: Shift to online news and possible third parties
segments.summary: Hosts discuss networks pivoting toward online video and podcasts, the aging baby boomer audience, and Chuck's hope that disillusionment with both parties could support third parties.

segments.title: Closing remarks
segments.summary: Chuck clarifies that the episode is not an attack on conservative or liberal listeners and the hosts sign off on the topic.

segments.title: Listener mail: Hindenburg follow-up
segments.summary: Katie, a wildlife biologist and longtime listener, writes about the Hindenburg episode, the Bend Dover joke, and listening on long drives. The hosts read the mail and invite listeners to send their own anecdotes.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Standard iHeartRadio production sign-off.
